_readme: Numbers for the extra features added on 2026-11-14 (the "more stuff" list: launch window, mission patch, clean room, lucky peanuts, weather call, zero-g toy, two-way fixes, window spotting and postcards, footprints, the vanishing Mars ice, the rocket line-up, tap a part, mostly fuel, ask the crew). The words are in data/story.json "extras" and data/inner_voice.json "extras". Real gravity is in data/destinations.json (arrival > gravity_scale) and the radio delay in destinations.json (signal_delay_minutes). Every made-up number is marked PLACEHOLDER until the team passes it.

launch_window._readme: The Launch window station in the Design Room (after the orbit). Each date: trip_factor = the trip takes this many times the mission's trip_days (a longer trip uses more food, water and air on the ship); effects = added to the six resources (mass = extra fuel for a poorer path); tightness_factor = the launch rings' tightness is multiplied by this (bigger = smaller timing windows; the best date has a short window, so the launch moments are tighter; a poor date has a wide one). default = the date used before the player picks one (it changes nothing, so old builds stay the same).
launch_window._scrub_readme: UPGRADE_PLAN_V6 B1 (2026-11-15): effects budget = the money spent WAITING for that date (the best date is far away, the poor date is the soonest). scrub_chance = how likely the weather scrubs the launch (amber weather) each time you are on the pad; max_scrubs = the most scrubs in a row for that date. Waiting out a scrub costs weather > wait_cost each time. All PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice.
launch_window.source: trip_factor, effects and tightness_factor: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice (2026-11-14), waiting for the team's pass. mars_every_months: "about once every 26 months they are aligned in a way that allows the most energy-efficient trip to Mars": https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/timeline/launch/launch-windows/ (also https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-suspends-2016-launch-of-insight-mission-to-mars/: "only a few weeks every 26 months"). Moon windows: NASA Artemis II, "approximately one week of launch opportunities, followed by three weeks without": https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/artemis-ii-mission-availability.pdf

patch._readme: NOT USED since 2026-11-14 (UPGRADE_PLAN_V3 A1 removed the patch everywhere; the maker is in scenes/archive and scripts/archive). The mission patch maker (scenes/patch_maker.tscn). shapes, icons = the choices (their names are in story.json extras > patch). colors = the patch colors to pick from. default = the patch before the player makes one. texture_pixels = how big the patch picture is when it goes on the rocket and the suit. preview_pixels = the big patch on the maker screen. suit_patch_meters = the patch's size on the suit.

peanuts._readme: The lucky peanut jar on the launch screen. jar_count = peanuts in the jar. They change nothing in the game.
peanuts.source: jar_count: game-design choice. since_year: JPL's lucky peanuts started with Ranger 7 on July 28, 1964: https://science.nasa.gov/missions/what-are-jpls-lucky-peanuts/

weather._readme: The wait-or-go weather call on the launch pad. amber_chance = how often the weather is amber (0 to 1). On amber, GO FOR LAUNCH asks: launch now (the launch rings get tighter: tightness x go_tightness_factor) or wait a day (wait_cost million $ come out of the cash reserve for the flight, and the weather turns green).
weather.source: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice (2026-11-14), waiting for the team's pass.

zero_g_toy._readme: The little plush that floats up on the Bridge when the flight starts (a zero-g indicator). position = where it floats [x, y, z] (ship map, game_data.json ship); rise_seconds = how long it takes to float up from the console; bob_meters and spin_degrees_per_second = how it drifts. Colors are web color codes. Looks only.
zero_g_toy.source: Look: game-design choice. The idea: crews fly a small plush toy as a zero-gravity indicator (ZGI), for example the Artemis II mascot "Rise": https://www.nasa.gov/general/moonmascot/ and a Soyuz crew's toy cat: https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/cosmonaut-oleg-novitskiy-holds-up-zero-g-indicator/

two_way_fix._readme: Every ship emergency has two fixes. Proper fix: hold E for proper_hold_seconds (it costs nothing). Quick fix: press Q, done at once, but it costs something later: at the end of the trip the flight log says what. quick_costs: event = a design emergency costs data_gb of data sent home; crew = a crew emergency costs cash million $ from the cash reserve.
two_way_fix.source: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice (2026-11-14), waiting for the team's pass.

spotting._readme: Window spotting and postcards on the ship. Stand near a window (window_reach_meters), look at Earth, the Moon, the Sun or the destination (within look_degrees) and press E: a sighting is collected and a postcard (a photo of the view) is saved for the report (at most max_postcards). Earth sits behind the ship (seen from the back windows) and shrinks during the trip from earth_start_degrees to earth_end_degrees on screen; the Moon sits next to it. The Sun is far off to one side. Sizes and colors: looks only.
spotting._earth_swing_readme: 2026-11-15 team note: first you see Earth, then the destination. earth_swing: Earth starts big in the Bridge window (front_right_degrees to the right, front_down_degrees below eye level), then swings out past the right-hand windows (side_x meters to the side) and ends behind the ship by 'until' (share of the trip, 0 to 1). Set until to 0 for the old look (Earth always behind).
spotting._satellites_readme: Satellites that drift past the windows while the ship is still near Earth (the first 'until' share of the trip). count = how many; side_min / side_max = meters to the left or right of the ship's middle (outside the 9.5 m walls); start_ahead = how far in front the first one starts; gap = extra distance between them. Colors: looks only.

ask_crew._readme: Ask the crew: the staff carry a "?" bubble; stand within reach_meters of one and press E for one line about the room they are in (story.json extras > ask_crew). bubble_height = how high the "?" floats over their feet.

footprints._readme: Footprints on the planet. spacing_meters = a print every this many meters walked; size = [width, length] of one print in meters; max_prints = the most prints kept (the oldest goes first). life_seconds per destination: 0 = they stay forever (the Moon has no wind), a number = they fade away in that many seconds (Mars has wind). color_darken = how much darker than the ground a print is (0 to 1).
footprints.source: spacing, size, max_prints, color_darken and the 25-second Mars fade: game-design choice. Moon prints staying: "Barring a chance meteorite impact, these impressions in the lunar soil will probably last for millions of years": https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/lunar/apollo_11_30th.html; "there is no wind or rain to erode the surface" (LRO still sees Apollo tracks): https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/moon/10-cool-things-nasas-lunar-reconnaissance-orbiter-is-teaching-us-about-the-moon/

ice_race._readme: Race the ice (Mars): after_task = the task that drills the ice, send_task = the analyzer task. Once the ice is drilled, the sample slowly turns to gas. vanish_seconds = how long until it is gone; the analyze task then sends data_gb x the share of ice left, never less than min_share. carry_size = the ice cube's size in meters, floating by the player.
ice_race.source: vanish_seconds, min_share: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice (2026-11-14). The idea: in June 2008 "dice-size crumbs of bright material have vanished from inside a trench" dug by Phoenix; it was water ice that sublimated over four days: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/bright-chunks-at-phoenix-landers-mars-site-must-have-been-ice/

rocket_lineup._readme: The rocket line-up in the Design Room: a school bus stands by each rocket, at the same scale, so its size makes sense. real_height_meters = each rocket's real height; bus = a school bus's real size [length, height, width] in meters. Colors: looks only.
rocket_lineup.source: Falcon 9: "70 meters (229.6 feet)": https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/spaceships-and-rockets/commercial-crew-rockets/; Atlas V 401: "188 feet (57.3 meters)": https://science.nasa.gov/resource/atlas-v-401-rocket/; Atlas V 541 (Mars 2020): "about 197 feet (60 meters)": https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mars_2020/launch/mission/; bus length 13.2 m: Hubble is 43.5 feet long, "about the size of a school bus": https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/observatory/design/ (the bus height and width are game-design choices, look only).

tap_part._readme: Tap a part: in the Design Room's Inside view, click a part of the spacecraft on the display stand for its job in five words. pick_pixels = how close to the middle of the screen (where you look) a part must be.

mostly_fuel._readme: The Fueling gauge also shows how much of a rocket's weight on the pad is fuel (fuel_share per rocket, 0 to 1).
mostly_fuel.source: NASA: "the most cleverly engineered, efficient rocket is still about 85% fuel by mass": https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter14-1/; full-scale rockets are "typically 80 – 85%" propellant: https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/model-rockets-and-real-rockets/ (the same 85% for each rocket: no per-rocket NASA figure was found).

clean_room._readme: The Clean Room: since 2026-11-14 it is a task HALFWAY THROUGH THE FLIGHT, not a build job. At flight_at (0-1 of the trip) a yellow task opens at flight_station; walking there and pressing E opens the minigame on top of the ship (the trip pauses while you clean). Dust specks land on the instrument; hold the mouse button and wipe them off before time runs out. duration_seconds = one turn; specks = how many land in one turn; spawn_every_seconds = a new speck this often; wipe_radius_pixels = the cloth's size; speck_size_pixels = how big a speck is. Score = specks wiped / specks x 100. The team average becomes CLEANLINESS (it counts in the teamwork score). If the ship arrives and nobody cleaned, CLEANLINESS is missed_score. Skipping the trip (Enter, after the first trip) costs nothing.
clean_room.source: Numbers: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice (2026-11-14), waiting for the team's pass. The idea: spacecraft are assembled in clean rooms with strict cleaning to keep Earth microbes off them (planetary protection): https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/docs/MSL%20Plan%20Prot%20Fact%20Sheet%20ApprovedRev1%208-3-12.pdf and https://planetaryprotection.jpl.nasa.gov/research
